title: Idle timers, waking and session limits
standfirst: An always-available agent depends on three separate settings: a lifetime deadline, an idle timer, and a wake path. Providers bundle them differently, and the difference is most of your bill.
idea: A lifetime limit is a hard deadline counted from creation or last resume. It ends the machine even if it is busy. An idle timer parks the machine when nothing is happening. A wake path decides whether the next request brings it back, or whether someone has to start it.

A provider can pass two of the three and fail the use case. Boat has no idle timer and still stops your box after an hour, because its deadline counts from creation. Lizard never sleeps for idleness and deletes the sandbox five minutes after creation if you used the SDK. Agent 37 never stops on its own, but it also never wakes itself if you stopped it.

What counts as activity is the quiet variable. Runtime counts an open terminal or SSH session. Sprites counts an in-flight request, output to a session, an open TCP connection or an active task. boxd counts TCP/UDP traffic in either direction, so polling an API keeps a machine awake while a local compile does not.

splits.heading: The timer counts from creation, not from use
body: Boat's auto-stop counts from creation or the last resume and defaults to one hour. A running agent prompt pushes the deadline out by one TTL, but ordinary work does not. E2B's timeout is also a countdown: running commands and requests to the sandbox URL do not reset it, and the default action is to kill the sandbox.

Vercel has no published idle timer at all, only a session timeout: 45 minutes on Hobby and 24 hours on Pro. A long-idle sandbox is not stopped for being idle; it is stopped when the session limit arrives.

splits.heading: Sleep can be automatic and invisible
body: Sprites pauses after about 30 seconds without activity, then stops the VM and drops memory after a longer idle period that is not published. Blaxel's docs say standby after 15 minutes of idle connection; its pricing page says scale-to-zero after about five seconds. Morph's devboxes sleep after inactivity, and Runtime pauses after five minutes by default.

The wake path matters as much as the timer. Sprites wakes on a request to its URL, Runtime on the next command or request, InstaBox on a public-port visit, and Agent 37 on any request to any URL. Boat cannot wake on a URL at all, because a stop destroyed the machine.

splits.heading: The idle hour is where the bill lives
body: An idle hour can cost full compute, memory only, storage only, or nothing. boxd's standby bills RAM. Runtime bills memory and disk blocks. Agent 37, InstaBox and Lizard bill storage only. Boat charges nothing while stopped and keeps the disk for 14 days.

That is why two providers with similar hourly rates differ by a factor of ten on an always-on box. A 4 vCPU / 8 GiB machine costs about $10.60 a month at Agent 37, $26.28 at Boat, $27.23 at InstaBox and about $222 at boxd once memory is billed on a 4 vCPU machine.

watchFor: Whether the deadline counts from creation, from last activity, or from network traffic.
What counts as activity: data flow, an open connection, a terminal, or a running command.
Whether a sleeping machine wakes on a request, and how long the wake takes.
Whether an idle hour bills compute, memory, storage, or nothing.
Whether the timer can be turned off or only raised.

rows.scenario: Still running and still billing: nothing pauses it unless you opt in to auto-sleep.
rows.note: No lifetime cap, and auto-sleep is off by default, so a box stays up and bills compute by the minute until you stop or delete it. Any request to any URL wakes a sleeping instance.

source.quote: Instances default to `auto_sleep: false` and never sleep on their own unless you opt them in.

rows.scenario: Asleep after 15 minutes of idle connection, or about five seconds if the pricing page is right; the next request resumes it.
rows.note: Standby after 15 minutes of idle WebSocket or TCP activity according to the docs, or about 5 seconds according to the pricing page. Resume from standby is claimed under 25 ms.

source.quote: if the WebSocket/TCP connection remains idle for 15 minutes with no activity, the sandbox will automatically transition to standby mode.

rows.scenario: Awake at 00:20, because the clock counts from creation, not activity; it stops at the one-hour mark whether or not the work is finished.
rows.note: No idle detection, but a hard auto-stop counts from create or resume: one hour by default, 30 days maximum, and off is allowed. A stop destroys the machine, so a URL cannot wake it.

source.quote: The default is 1 hour.

rows.scenario: Awake: hibernation needs four hours without TCP or UDP traffic, and a stalled model call makes none.
rows.note: Runtime is unlimited and auto-suspend is off by default. Auto-hibernate is on by default after four hours without TCP/UDP traffic in either direction, so outbound polling keeps a box awake but a local compile does not.

source.quote: **On by default, set to 4 hours.** After 4 hours without TCP/UDP traffic in either direction, boxd hibernates the machine

rows.scenario: Still running at 20 minutes if the Durable Object stays active; if it goes inactive the instance stops shortly after, unless a timeout of up to 6 hours was set.
rows.note: No default inactivity timeout in Sandboxes 1.0, a 6-hour maximum, and the value is lost on a Durable Object restart. Code inside does not count as activity. The 10-minute default belongs to the legacy 0.x SDK.

source.quote: After the Durable Object becomes inactive, the instance keeps running for the time set with `setInactivityTimeout()`, up to 6 hours.

rows.scenario: Stops at 15 minutes even mid-build, because only external calls reset the timer; the VM class would pause at 60 minutes instead.
rows.note: Container and GPU auto-stop after 15 idle minutes by default; VM classes auto-pause after 60. Only lifecycle calls, preview requests, SSH and Toolbox calls reset it. An optional TTL destroys in any state; a stopped container archives after 7 days.

source.quote: if not set, the default interval of 15 minutes is used

rows.scenario: Killed at the five-minute timeout, losing the queued test run; a pause would have kept memory, but pausing is opt-in.
rows.note: A timeout defaults to five minutes and kills the sandbox; pausing instead is opt-in. Commands and URL requests do not reset it. Continuous runtime is capped at one hour on Hobby and 24 hours on Pro.

source.quote: Every sandbox has a timeout, and it defaults to **5 minutes** if you do not set one.

rows.scenario: Still running at 00:20, paused at 00:30, and woken by the command at 01:00 with the process intact.
rows.note: Paid machines have no lifetime timeout, but idle auto-pause defaults to 30 minutes; paid plans can choose 5–30 minutes or off. Nothing deletes a paused or stopped machine: there is no forced TTL.

source.quote: A new machine pauses once it has been idle for 30 minutes.

rows.scenario: Already gone: there is no idle timer, and a sandbox made through the SDK expires five minutes after creation.
rows.note: There is no idle timer at all, but every sandbox has a hard lifetime deadline: five minutes by default from the SDK and CLI, and never by default from the dashboard and raw API.

source.quote: Five minutes by default from the SDK and CLI; no expiration by default from the raw API and dashboard

rows.scenario: Terminated at the five-minute default lifetime before the model answers, unless the timeout was raised to at most 24 hours.
rows.note: Default maximum lifetime 5 minutes, up to 24 hours. Idle timeout is off by default and terminates rather than pauses. There is no lifetime-free option; longer work needs snapshots.

source.quote: Sandboxes have a default maximum lifetime of 5 minutes.

rows.scenario: Scaled to zero after an unpublished period of inactivity, with memory preserved; the 01:00 request wakes it.
rows.note: Devboxes scale to zero after inactivity, preserving memory and application state, and wake on an HTTP or SSH request. Instance TTL is a duration after which an instance stops or pauses.

source.quote: Devboxes can branch to hundreds of parallel replicas or scale to zero after a period of inactivity, preserving all application and memory state.

rows.scenario: Paused at five minutes, woken by the 01:00 command in about a second, process and memory intact.
rows.note: No clock unless you set one, and `persistent: true` disables the idle pause. Otherwise it pauses after five idle minutes and wakes on the next request, usually within a second.

source.quote: A sandbox pauses itself after 300 seconds with nothing happening in it: no request, no command still running, no open connection, no network traffic and no CPU use.

rows.scenario: Paused at 15 minutes on the lowest plan and later on higher ones; the one-hour auto-stop then stops it with memory and disk kept.
rows.note: No maximum lifetime, but a hard auto-stop defaults to one hour and idle pause to 15–120 minutes by plan. An always-on box needs `ttlSeconds: null` and `idleStopMinutes: 0`.

source.quote: `ttlSeconds` | 1 s – 30 days, or `null`

rows.scenario: Paused after about 30 seconds; the 01:00 command resumes warm memory in 100–500 ms.
rows.note: A warm pause after about 30 seconds idle, a cold stop after a longer unpublished period, and wake on request. Four things reset the timer, including an open TCP connection.

source.quote: When the activity stops, a short idle window passes (about 30 seconds today) and the Sprite pauses.

rows.scenario: Stopped at the five-minute session timeout; the next command starts a new session from the saved filesystem, not from memory.
rows.note: A session timeout of five minutes by default, with a maximum session of 45 minutes on Hobby and 24 hours on Pro. No idle-activity timer is published.

source.quote: Sandboxes automatically stop after a timeout. The default timeout is 5 minutes

rows.scenario: Ten minutes without proxied traffic suspends a named sandbox and deletes an ephemeral one; the plan caps the window at 2 hours, 24 hours or not at all.
rows.note: `timeout_secs` is an idle threshold measured on proxy traffic — SSH, a PTY WebSocket, an exposed port, an SDK call — not a wall-clock lifetime. Default 600 s; maximum 2 h on Free, 24 h with Usage Credits, unlimited on Pro. Setting 0 requests the plan maximum.

source.quote: If `timeout_secs` is not set, it goes with the default value which is `600` sec (10 minutes).

rows.figure: No idle stop; runs for weeks
rows.scenario: Nothing idles a Droplet: it stays up for weeks until you power it off or destroy it.
rows.note: No idle timer, no session lifetime and no wake-on-request for a Droplet; billing starts at create and ends at destroy. Managed Agents is the opposite: a 15-minute idle suspend by default, resuming on new input.

source.quote: Billing begins when you create the Droplet and ends when you destroy it.

rows.scenario: The agent is still awake at 00:20, because there is no idle timer and no lifetime limit to configure; nothing stops it but you.
rows.note: There is no idle timeout, no auto-stop and no maximum session length, so an always-on agent is safe from the provider. The same absence means there is no wake path: a server that is powered off stays off until something calls the API, and a stopped server cannot be woken by a request.

source.quote: We will bill you for each cloud server until you choose to delete them.

rows.scenario: Still running at 00:20 and at 01:00; nothing pauses it for idleness, and the plan keeps billing.
rows.note: No idle timer and no lifetime cap: a VPS runs until you stop it or the subscription ends. That is good for an always-on agent, but there is no idle setting to choose and no wake-on-request, so an idle machine cannot be made cheaper.

source.quote: This is a compute-only power state change and does not affect billing.

rows.scenario: Leave it idle: set idleTimeoutSeconds and the VM pauses, then the next request wakes it; set −1 to keep it awake.
rows.note: A paused VM resumes on the next start or on traffic that reaches it. No scheduler: cron inside the VM only runs while it runs.

source.quote: A VM paused this way resumes on its next start, or on the next traffic that reaches it.

rows.scenario: Nothing puts the server to sleep: an agent that waits all day keeps its process and its connection.
rows.note: There is no idle timer, no automatic sleep and no session length limit — the server runs until you stop it or cancel the plan, which is what a Discord gateway or an always-on Hermes agent needs. The trade is that idle hours are billed like busy ones. There is also no provider-side scheduler: recurring work runs from cron inside the guest, and the only schedule HostUp runs is the backup one.

source.quote: A standard VPS is paid for one month or one year at a time.

scenario.title: Mid-refactor, 20 minutes of silence
scenario.setup: Your agent is 40 minutes into a refactor on a 4 vCPU / 8 GB box. It has written six files, a test run is queued in memory, and the model call stalls. Nothing touches the machine for 20 minutes.

beats.what: The last command returns. The agent waits on the model, so no request, command or CPU use reaches the sandbox.
Still silent. Whether the machine is running, frozen or already gone depends entirely on the provider's default, not on anything you set.
The model answers and the agent sends its next command.

scenario.turn: At 00:20 the provider keeps the machine, freezes it, or has ended it. At 01:00 the bill and the work diverge: a frozen machine resumes in place, a stopped one has lost the queued process, and a killed one returns an error.

questions: When the timer fires, does the machine pause with memory, stop and keep the disk, or get deleted — and which of those does the provider call stop?
Does the clock count from creation, from the last command, or from any network traffic, and does an open SSH session reset it?
Can the idle timer be turned off, or only raised to a maximum — and what is that maximum?
What does an idle hour cost in each state, and does a paused machine keep billing memory?
After a pause, how long does the first request wait, and do open connections and running processes survive?
